title: The family table: where the day gets told
description: Dinner is rarely just dinner. Around a shared table, the small events of separate days become family knowledge — and that quiet exchange does more work than it looks like.

body.heading: News travels at the table
paragraphs: Families spend their days apart — school, work, errands, screens. The shared meal is often the one reliable hour when everyone's news can be pooled: the test result, the funny thing the bus driver said, the worry that has been carried around all day.

Children who regularly hear adults talk through ordinary problems at the table absorb something valuable: how people describe a difficulty, disagree kindly and make a plan, in real sentences, at normal volume.

body.heading: Protect the hour lightly
paragraphs: The table works best unforced. Phones in another room help; interrogation does not. One open question — what was the strangest part of your day? — usually opens more doors than a round of reports.
It does not need to be dinner, or daily, or everyone. A weekend breakfast or a shared snack after school can carry the same conversation. The meal is the excuse; the telling is the point.

takeaway: A shared meal is the family's daily news exchange: protect the hour lightly, ask one open question, and let the day get told.
